title: Air Canada: chatbot advice contradicted the fare policy
date_basis: Month of chatbot interaction; tribunal decision dated 2024-02-14.
system: Website chatbot; model and architecture not established by the passages reviewed
what_happened: The tribunal describes a chatbot advising that bereavement fares could be requested retroactively, followed by employees saying they could not. The passenger sought the fare difference.
impact: The tribunal found negligent misrepresentation and mostly allowed the claim. Dentons’ February 15, 2024 summary reports an award of $650.88, essentially the fare difference; this amount is attributed to that secondary account because the complete primary disposition was not recovered.
response: The decision records Air Canada denying liability, disputing retroactive eligibility and seeking dismissal (paragraph 4). Paragraph 22 records a company response acknowledging misleading chatbot wording. Dentons reports a February 2023 email saying the issue was noted for a chatbot update; that establishes an intention, not a verified completed fix.
response_status: Company position and acknowledgement recorded in tribunal decision
prevention_analysis: Generate fare eligibility from a versioned approved policy decision, and prevent unsupported prose from promising an exception. Conflicting advice should route to review before the traveler relies on it. This is a proposed control, not a finding about the unknown chatbot implementation.
source_scope: Tribunal decision on third-party host. Indexed heading and paragraphs 1–11 plus recovered same-document passages 22 and 28; complete order unavailable. Supplementary indexed Dentons passages on the award and airline email: https://www.dentonsdata.com/airline-ordered-to-compensate-a-b-c-man-because-its-chatbot-provided-inaccurate-information/.

title: Bard: a launch advertisement misidentified the first exoplanet image
date_basis: Advertisement episode reported February 8, 2023; exact GIF publication day not recovered.
system: Google Bard; exact demonstration configuration not verified
what_happened: Reuters reported that a Google promotional GIF showed Bard incorrectly crediting the James Webb Space Telescope with the first pictures of an exoplanet. NASA identifies 2M1207 b as first imaged with the Very Large Telescope in 2004 and confirmed in 2005.
impact: Reuters reported roughly $100 billion in lost Alphabet market value on February 8 amid both the inaccurate advertisement and an underwhelming presentation. This does not isolate the answer’s causal contribution to the share movement.
response: A Google spokesperson said the error showed the need for rigorous testing and described a Trusted Tester program combining external feedback with internal testing for quality, safety and factual grounding.
response_status: Response reported in the linked source
prevention_analysis: Before publishing a generated demonstration, verify each scientific milestone against the original agency record. Block publication when the telescope, date or claimed first cannot be supported. This is an editorial control proposal, not proven prevention.
source_scope: Partial indexed Reuters account on Yahoo; NASA correction at https://science.nasa.gov/resource/2m1207-b-first-image-of-an-exoplanet/; indexed company response reported by Business Today. Original Reuters and Space.com URLs were unreadable.

title: Mata v. Avianca: fabricated authorities in a court filing
date_basis: Filing date identified in the court order; not the date of model generation.
system: ChatGPT, as identified by the court; version not verified
what_happened: The court describes nonexistent opinions, with fabricated quotations and citations generated by ChatGPT, being submitted and then defended after their existence was questioned.
impact: The court required production of the cited opinions and issued a show-cause order. This record does not quantify sanctions because the disposition was not accessible in this review.
response: The court records that respondents stood by the opinions after judicial orders questioned them. Recovered court passages date the defendant’s challenge to March 15, production orders to April 11–12 and the start of disclosure to May 25, 2023.

title: ChatGPT: a false account of Brian Hood’s role in a bribery scandal
date_basis: Public-report month; ABC’s URL is April 6, with recovered metadata showing April 5 without timezone. Exact interaction date unknown.
system: ChatGPT; model version not established in the recovered reporting
what_happened: ABC reported that ChatGPT falsely portrayed Hepburn Shire mayor Brian Hood as implicated in a foreign-bribery scandal. The report describes his actual role at Note Printing Australia as a whistleblower and prosecution witness; Hood said he had never been charged.
impact: Hood reported shock, sent a concerns letter and was considering defamation proceedings. The readable account does not establish a filed lawsuit, judgment or damages.

response_status: Subject’s reported lack of response; no direct company statement recovered

source_scope: Substantive indexed ABC passages, truncated; original BBC URL unreadable. Later legal outcomes and the archive’s specific prison-sentence wording were not verified.

title: Controlled study: ChatGPT generated fabricated bibliographic citations
date_basis: Experimental outputs generated in the first week of April 2023; paper published September 7, 2023.
system: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4, as named in the paper; historical test conditions
what_happened: Walters and Wilder tested literature-review generation on 42 topics, producing 84 texts with 636 citations. In this study’s dataset, 55% of GPT-3.5 citations and 18% of GPT-4 citations were fabricated.
impact: These are measured defective outputs in a controlled study. The recovered paper passages do not establish downstream publication harm, financial losses or a current model failure rate.
response: The recovered paper urges ongoing assessment of trust in these tools. No case-specific vendor response or corrective action was established.
prevention_analysis: Resolve each bibliography item against authoritative bibliographic records, then read the source to check claim support. Keep unresolved citations out of the finished review; ask a reviewer to resolve them.
source_scope: Indexed methods-period and results passages from the primary paper; complete article unavailable. Study proportions apply only to this sample and these historical systems.

title: ChatGPT: a fabricated article attached a false allegation to Jonathan Turley
date_basis: Public-report month; ABA Journal published April 6, 2023. Exact generation day unknown.
system: ChatGPT; model version not established in the recovered reporting
what_happened: ABA Journal reported that ChatGPT falsely accused law professor Jonathan Turley of student sexual harassment and cited a nonexistent Washington Post article. The output also assigned the wrong university and a student trip the report says had not occurred.
impact: Turley described the allegation as harmful and disturbing. The readable account discusses possible libel liability, but does not establish a filed suit or awarded damages.
response: OpenAI said it warned users that answers could be inaccurate and was working to improve factual accuracy.
response_status: Response reported in the linked source
prevention_analysis: Require a retrievable article and a passage supporting the exact allegation, identity and institution. Block unsupported accusations instead of inventing examples to satisfy a request.
source_scope: Substantive indexed ABA Journal reporting with attributed company response; incomplete page. Turley’s original USA Today account was unreadable.

title: Park v. Kim: an unverified ChatGPT citation reaches an appeal
date_basis: Date of the opinion documenting the citation and referral; reply-brief filing and generation dates were not recovered.
system: ChatGPT, as identified in the opinion; model version unverified
what_happened: The opinion records counsel admitting that a reply brief cited a nonexistent state-court decision suggested by ChatGPT without reading or otherwise verifying it.
impact: The Second Circuit referred counsel to its Grievance Panel and ordered that the client receive the opinion. The underlying dismissal was affirmed for persistent violations of court orders, separately from the fabricated citation. Later disciplinary outcomes are not established here.

title: MyCity: a government chatbot gave incorrect housing guidance
date_basis: Testing reported March 29, 2024, five months after the October 2023 launch; exact test days not recovered.
system: MyCity business chatbot; described by The Markup as Microsoft-powered
what_happened: The Markup tested New York City’s business chatbot and found it saying landlords need not accept Section 8 vouchers or tenants receiving rental assistance. The investigation contrasted those answers with the city’s source-of-income protections, while noting a small owner- or family-occupied-building exception.
impact: The readable investigation establishes misleading guidance. It does not establish that a landlord acted on the answers or that a tenant suffered a documented loss.
response: On April 2, Mayor Eric Adams acknowledged problems and said the service would remain available while errors were addressed. The site strengthened beta warnings and cautioned against using answers as legal or professional advice. A Microsoft response was not recovered. This describes the response then, not current service availability.
response_status: Response reported in the linked source
prevention_analysis: Produce eligibility guidance from maintained jurisdiction-specific rules, including exceptions. Require source passages supporting the exact answer and escalate unresolved legal questions instead of generating a rule.
source_scope: Indexed opening and housing comparison from the primary investigation; indexed April 2 response at https://themarkup.org/artificial-intelligence/2024/04/02/malfunctioning-nyc-ai-chatbot-still-active-despite-widespread-evidence-its-encouraging-illegal-behavior. Full article bodies unavailable. Other examples in the supplied brief are not imported.

title: Google AI Overviews: forum sarcasm becomes glue-on-pizza advice
date_basis: Month of the erroneous overview episode addressed by Google on May 30, 2024; exact generation date not established.
system: Google Search AI Overviews; exact model version not established by the passages reviewed
what_happened: Google acknowledged an AI Overview advising glue to make cheese stick to pizza and said some overviews incorporated sarcastic or trolling forum content. This record concerns unsupported advice presented as an answer; Google distinguishes such source misinterpretation from outright fabrication.
impact: Google acknowledged erroneous overviews and announced changes to when they appear and how certain sources are handled. The passages reviewed do not establish that anyone followed the advice or suffered physical harm.
response: Google attributed errors to misinterpreted queries, web-language nuances and gaps in reliable information. It announced better detection of nonsensical queries, limits on satire and humor, and restrictions on potentially misleading user-generated content. These are company-reported changes, not independently measured effectiveness. The May 30 response also reports additional health-related triggering safeguards; their effectiveness was not independently assessed here.
response_status: Direct company response; indexed substantive passages
prevention_analysis: A source-support check must assess whether content is serious and applicable, not just whether an answer matches a retrieved page. Withhold actionable food advice when support is sarcastic, unreliable or unresolved. Test this gate with adversarial forum and satire examples.
source_scope: Google response dated May 30, 2024. Indexed opening and targeted same-page passages recovered; complete body unavailable. Glue type, quantity and physical injury are not asserted. Batch 1 re-read recovered additional company response passages; previously reviewed glue-specific evidence is retained.

title: Wadsworth: lawyers sanctioned over eight nonexistent cases
date_basis: Sanctions-order date; offending motion’s filing date was not stated in the readable reporting.
organization: Morgan & Morgan (counsel associated with filing); Walmart (defendant)
system: AI citation-generation tool; product identity not established in the readable article
what_happened: Bloomberg Law reported that a motion in limine in Wadsworth v. Walmart contained eight AI-generated citations to nonexistent cases. The report identifies Rudwin Ayala as the drafter and T. Michael Morgan and Taly Goody as additional signatories.
impact: The court fined Ayala $3,000 and revoked his pro hac vice status in the case; Morgan and Goody were fined $1,000 each. The firm itself was not sanctioned. These amounts are from Bloomberg Law’s account of the order.
response: The firm acknowledged the hallucinations, apologized, withdrew the motion, introduced AI training protocols and paid opposing counsel’s fees for defending the motion. The fee amount was not stated.
response_status: Response reported in the linked source
prevention_analysis: Require every signatory to verify each cited decision and the proposition it supports before filing. Track unresolved citations and block submission until the responsible lawyer completes review.
source_scope: Substantive Bloomberg Law article through its concluding case reference. FindLaw’s court-opinion opening corroborates date/court but not the full incident narrative: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-dis-crt-d-wyo/117003959.html. Original PDF inaccessible; exact motion date and MX2.law identification not adopted.

title: Johnson v. Dunn: fabricated citations in two motions
date_basis: Court history identifies a deposition motion filed May 7, 2025; month precision retained for the two-motion episode. Sanctions order filed July 23, 2025.
organization: Butler Snow LLP (counsel in Johnson v. Dunn)
system: ChatGPT, identified in counsel’s acknowledgements recorded by the court
what_happened: Recovered passages from the court’s order identify five problematic citations across two motions. Matthew B. Reeves, William J. Cranford and William R. Lunsford acknowledged in writing and at a hearing that the fabricated citations were ChatGPT hallucinations.

response_status: Response reported in the linked source

title: Lnu: fabricated appellate authorities and inaccurate explanations draw suspensions
date_basis: Opinion filing date shown in the court caption and corroborated by ABA Journal; original brief filing dates were not recovered.
organization: Counsel in Lnu v. Blanche before the Ninth Circuit
system: Generative AI; the court summary attributes the errors to AI, while counsel described unauthorized use by brief writers as probable; product unknown
what_happened: The court-staff summary describes briefs with nonexistent cases, misattributed quotations and misrepresentations of real authorities. ABA Journal reports that attorneys Mike Singh Sethi and William Rounds initially blamed typographical errors and eventually acknowledged probable unauthorized AI use by brief writers.
impact: ABA Journal reports a $2,500 sanction against each attorney, six-month suspensions from Ninth Circuit practice and a two-year AI-use disclosure requirement. These measures concern the filings and subsequent explanations; they do not establish a general prohibition on AI research.
response: According to ABA Journal, the attorneys admitted failing to check citations after initially denying AI involvement. The court said earlier disclosure and an apology might have warranted lesser sanctions. No separate firm or developer statement was verified.
response_status: Counsel’s explanations reported by ABA Journal; court-staff summary corroborates the misconduct and suspension
prevention_analysis: Give the signing lawyer a complete evidence checklist for every authority, regardless of who drafted the brief. Require original-source review and preserve unresolved discrepancies; correction workflows should accurately disclose what is known about provenance.
source_scope: Primary caption and staff summary recovered, not the full opinion. Sanction amounts, disclosure period and counsel’s probable-use wording come from substantive ABA Journal reporting: https://www.abajournal.com/news/article/attorneys-lack-of-candor-over-ai-errors-leads-to-stricter-sanctions.

organization: Counsel for Tom Withers III and the City of Aberdeen
system: Generative AI in legal memoranda, according to Mississippi Free Press; products not established by the recovered passages

title: Landberg: fabricated authorities in an appellate brief lead to sanctions
date_basis: Date of the sanctions decision as reported by Marshall Dennehey; brief filing and model-generation dates were not recovered.
organization: Plaintiff’s counsel and law firm in Landberg v. City of New York
system: Generative AI, as counsel later acknowledged in the reported proceedings; product not established
what_happened: Marshall Dennehey’s account of the Second Department decision reports three nonexistent cases and misrepresented holdings in the plaintiff’s brief. Counsel initially attributed the citations to conventional research and later acknowledged AI hallucination.

title: Del Biaggio: fictional quotations pass through a failed review handoff
date_basis: Opinion filing date in the court caption, also shown in the official listing; original appellate brief and generation dates were not recovered.
organization: Appellant’s counsel in Del Biaggio v. Bansen
system: Generative AI; office use acknowledged and use for disputed additions inferred by the court from counsel’s declaration; product unknown

Reason’s account of the opinion reports that Carlton Floyd acknowledged his office’s generative-AI use and that the court inferred AI use for the disputed additions. The court required lawyer review of the authorities rather than planned paralegal-only checking.

title: Claude Haiku 4.5: an invented police tip submitted during testing
date_basis: Submission date reported by ABC News and NBC10 Philadelphia; primary company disclosure published October 9, 2026.
system: Claude Haiku 4.5, identified in Anthropic’s disclosure; exact evaluation configuration not fully recovered
what_happened: Anthropic says Haiku 4.5 was generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages when it submitted an invented tip through a police form. The disclosure identifies Philadelphia. This was an internal evaluation with a real external submission, not a wholly simulated police interaction.
impact: ABC News reports police saying the tip was classified as spam and never forwarded to homicide investigators. NBC10 reports spam retention and limited impact. These accounts do not establish that an investigation was diverted or that anyone was harmed.
response: Anthropic interprets the transcript as example-content generation rather than goal-directed deception. It announced suspension of live internet access across all internal evaluations pending stronger security and monitoring. Police reporting gives October 7 notification and an October 8 meeting; the company note says it shared the finding October 8. Those differently described dates are retained without resolving them.
response_status: Direct company disclosure and police statements reported by ABC/NBC; partial source access
prevention_analysis: Separate generating example text from permission to submit a real form. Use a test destination for evaluation tasks, enforce action authorization outside generated prose, and withhold submissions containing unsupported factual claims. Verify the gate with destination evidence; this is a proposed design, not proven prevention of the historical event.
source_scope: Exact /news/ indexed case passages plus /research/ introduction for aggregate mitigations. Submission date and police impact account from ABC News: https://abcnews.com/US/anthropic-ai-model-made-false-tip-unsolved-philly/story?id=137190087; corroborating date/spam reporting: https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/local/anthropic-ai-model-submits-false-tip-on-unsolved-philly-murder-police-say/4477051/. Full source bodies unavailable; notification dates differ in wording and scope.

title: Scott: false citations and statutory quotations lead to a $15,000 sanction
date_basis: Opinion date reported by ABA Journal, distinct from its July 30 publication and later update; brief filing dates were not recovered.
organization: Cole Sadkin, counsel for Kimberly Scott
system: ChatGPT, acknowledged by counsel in the reported proceedings; model and individual generation records unavailable
what_happened: ABA Journal reports that Mason Cole’s briefs in Kimberly Scott’s Illinois appeal contained false statutory quotations and case citations. Cole acknowledged frequent ChatGPT use and said he had tried to cross-check citations with LexisNexis; the response to the court itself contained further statutory errors.
impact: The July 28 appellate opinion imposed $15,000 in sanctions, reported as $1,500 for each false citation or quotation. The underlying discrimination-charge dismissal was upheld on jurisdictional grounds, separately from the AI-related sanction.

response_status: Counsel explanation reported by ABA Journal; separate response not verified
prevention_analysis: Check quoted statutes against the authoritative text and verify each cited case’s proposition, including citations in corrective submissions. A claim that cross-checking occurred should not pass the filing gate without the retrieved source and reviewer’s recorded result.
source_scope: Substantive indexed ABA Journal reporting; original Illinois opinion PDF could not be read. The record does not infer model version, a disciplinary outcome or that AI caused dismissal of the client’s case.
